examples: 200 photos named IMG_4521.jpg renamed 'Istanbul 001' to 'Istanbul 200' with the pattern Istanbul {n}.
Scanned invoices named Scan001.pdf renamed after their sender and date with What's inside.
Files with 'final_final' in their names tidied up with Find and Replace with.
action:Rename.worksOn: Files and folders; one or many.

action:Zip.summary: Packs files and folders into one ZIP archive, with an optional password.
action:Zip.details: Compress to ZIP opens with a name taken from the first item (Photos.zip, report.zip), which you can change. Choose Compression: Fast, Balanced (at first) or Smallest. 'Protect with a password' encrypts the files with AES-256; Windows 11, 7-Zip and WinRAR open such ZIPs, but File Explorer on Windows 10 can't. Create ZIP saves the archive in the folder of the first item, and the card shows its size.
action:Zip.how: Drag the files, tap Alt and drop on ZIP; name it and press Create ZIP.
examples: A project folder zipped into one file to upload to a client portal.
Tax documents zipped with a password before e-mailing them to an accountant.
Sixty photos packed into one ZIP so a friend downloads a single file.
action:Zip.worksOn: Files and folders; one or many.

action:CopyPath.summary: Copies the full path of each file as text, one path per line.
action:CopyPath.details: Copy Path puts the full location of the dropped files and folders on the clipboard as plain text, such as C:\Users\Sara\Documents\report.pdf. With several items each path goes on its own line. A card shows the path, or how many paths were copied.
action:CopyPath.how: Drag the files, tap Alt, open MORE and drop on COPY PATH, then paste the text where you need it.
examples: The path of a document on a shared drive pasted into an e-mail to a colleague.
A list of 40 file paths pasted into Excel for a project log.
A folder's path pasted into a program's Open box.
action:CopyPath.worksOn: Files and folders; one or many.

action:CopyName.summary: Copies file names as text, without their folders, one name per line.
action:CopyName.details: Copy Name puts just the names of the dropped files and folders on the clipboard, such as report.pdf, with the extension but without the folder they are in. With several items each name goes on its own line. A card shows the name, or how many names were copied.
action:CopyName.how: Drag the files, tap Alt, open MORE and drop on COPY NAME, then paste the names.
examples: The names of 25 photos pasted into a message so the client can say which ones they want.
A list of song files pasted into a note for a playlist.
A document's exact file name pasted into an e-mail subject.
action:CopyName.worksOn: Files and folders; one or many.

action:OpenWith.summary: Opens the files in a program you choose, all at once, without changing any default.
action:OpenWith.details: Open With lists the programs Windows suggests for the dropped files; choosing one opens every file in it at once, as File Explorer does for a selection. Another Program… lets you pick any program on the PC, and with a single file Windows' own chooser is offered too. Nothing becomes a default, so double-clicking still opens files the usual way.
action:OpenWith.how: Drag the files, tap Alt and drop on OPEN WITH, then pick the program.
examples: Ten photos opened together in Photoshop instead of the Photos app.
A CSV opened once in Notepad to look at the raw text.
A PDF opened in a browser instead of the usual PDF reader.

action:OpenInCode.summary: Opens files or a folder in Visual Studio Code, all in one window.
action:OpenInCode.details: Open in VS Code starts Visual Studio Code with every dropped file and folder in one window. When VS Code isn't installed the petal is dim and dashed, and the centre of the wheel says so. It waits under More on the Alt wheel unless you put it on the wheel itself in Settings › Actions Wheel.
action:OpenInCode.how: Drag the files or folder, tap Alt, open MORE and drop on VS CODE.
examples: A downloaded project folder opened in VS Code to look at the code.
A config file and a log opened side by side in one VS Code window.
A website folder opened to edit its HTML.
action:OpenInCode.worksOn: Files and folders; one or many.

action:Terminal.summary: Opens Windows Terminal in a folder, or in the folder that holds a file.
action:Terminal.details: Terminal opens Windows Terminal already in the dropped folder, or in the folder that holds the dropped file; with several items it uses the first. When Windows Terminal isn't installed, PowerShell opens there instead, and the Command Prompt if that fails. It waits under More on the Alt wheel unless you put it on the wheel itself in Settings › Actions Wheel.
action:Terminal.how: Drag a folder or file, tap Alt, open MORE and drop on TERMINAL.
examples: A project folder opened in a terminal to run a build command.
The folder of a downloaded installer opened to run it with options.
A folder of videos opened in PowerShell to run an FFmpeg command on them.
action:Terminal.worksOn: One folder or file (with several, the first is used).

action:Duplicates.summary: Finds identical files and copies of photos or videos at another size, then moves the extras to the Recycle Bin.
action:Duplicates.details: Find Duplicates searches the dropped files and folders and shows sets of duplicates with how much space each set would free. Besides identical files it finds Similar photos and Similar videos (copies at another size or quality) and Similar shots (photos taken within two minutes of each other that look alike, keeping the sharpest); these and 'Include subfolders' are on at first. Under Select choose 'Keep the original or best copy', 'Keep the newest' or 'Keep the oldest', and every other copy is ticked; you can change the ticks, but at least one copy in each set must stay. Move to Recycle Bin removes the ticked files, and History can put them back.
action:Duplicates.how: Drag files or folders, tap Alt and drop on DUPES; check the ticks and press Move to Recycle Bin.
examples: A Pictures folder with the same holiday photos imported three times: free 6 GB.
Smaller copies of photos saved from WhatsApp found next to the originals.
Ten burst shots of the same moment reduced to the sharpest one.
action:Duplicates.worksOn: Files and folders; one or many.

kind:format.summary: Converts the dropped files to another format, such as JPG, WEBP, MP4, MP3, PDF or DOCX, saved beside them.
kind:format.details: The Shift wheel shows your starred favourites first, then every format the files can become; the centre names the format with a few words on what it is good for (AVIF · Smallest, same look) and, while you rest on a picture, sound or video format, how big the result will be. Results are saved next to the originals with the new extension (photo.heic gives photo.jpg), or in one folder if you choose that in Settings › Results; a dropped folder is converted into a copy beside it, such as 'Trip (WEBP)', and the original is never touched. Quality comes from Settings › Quality: Image quality (90 at first, for JPG, WEBP, HEIC and AVIF), Page images DPI (300), Video quality (Best, High, Balanced or Small; High at first), Audio kbps (256), GIF frame rate (15), GIF width (720) and Hardware video encoding. A favourite such as 'WEBP 1600' adds its own size and quality, and a dim, dashed format petal needs something first, such as Ghostscript or Office, which the centre names.
kind:format.how: Drag the files, tap Shift and drop on the petal of the format you want, such as JPG or MP4.
examples: iPhone HEIC photos that won't open on an old PC: drop them on JPG.
A screen recording turned into a GIF for a chat, or a WAV interview into an MP3.
A Word file saved as a PDF to send, or a PDF's pages saved as PNG pictures in a folder.
kind:format.worksOn: Pictures, videos, audio, documents, spreadsheets, slides, e-books, subtitles, archives and design files; one or many, or a folder.

kind:favourite.summary: Converts to a format you use often with your own size and quality, from a starred petal first on the wheel.
kind:favourite.details: A favourite is a format plus a longest side and a quality, such as 'WEBP 1600' or 'MP4 720p'; up to six can be made in Settings › Favourites with Add a Favourite…. Choose the Format, the Longest side (Keep the size, or 3840 down to 512 px for pictures; 4K, 1440p, 1080p, 720p or 480p for videos), the Quality (95 to 50 for JPG, WEBP, HEIC and AVIF; Best, High, Balanced or Small for video; 320 to 96 kbps for audio; or As in Settings) and an optional Name. Favourites sit first on the conversion wheel with a star, in the order set in Settings, and smaller files are never enlarged. They also work on files already in that format, making a smaller copy such as 'photo 1600px.jpg'.
kind:favourite.how: Add one in Settings › Favourites, then drag files, tap Shift and drop on its starred petal.
examples: 'WEBP 1600' for every picture you upload to your shop's website.
'MP4 720p' for videos you send to family, so they stay small.
'JPG 1600' to make big camera JPGs smaller without changing their format.
kind:favourite.worksOn: Pictures, videos, audio and other files the chosen format can be made from; one or many.

kind:recipe.summary: Runs several steps on the files as one petal, such as remove the background, resize, save as WEBP and zip.
kind:recipe.details: A recipe is made in Settings › Recipes with New Recipe…: give it a name and add steps from Convert, Resize, Rotate, Compress, Remove Background, Add Watermark, Clean for Sharing, Rename, Compress to ZIP, Combine into one PDF and Make Searchable. Steps run in order, each on what the one before made, and each step has its own settings, such as a format and size, an app to compress for, watermark text and position, or a name pattern. With 'Show it on the tools wheel' on, the recipe appears first on the Ctrl wheel whenever it fits the files. Results are saved beside the originals as 'name' plus the recipe's name; Ask DropWheel's Save as Recipe… makes recipes too, and the command line runs them with petal run.
kind:recipe.how: Make it in Settings › Recipes, then drag files, tap Ctrl and drop on the recipe's petal.
examples: 'Shop photo': remove the background, resize to 1080 px and save as WEBP, for every new product picture.
'For the accountant': combine scans into one PDF, make it searchable and zip it.
'Instagram': add your watermark and compress for Instagram in one drop.
kind:recipe.worksOn: Whatever its first step takes: pictures for Resize, Rotate or Remove Background, many kinds for Convert or Compress; one or many files.

kind:petal.summary: Runs a program of your own on the dropped files, described by a small file in the petals folder.
kind:petal.details: Your own petals are small JSON files in %APPDATA%\Petal\petals; Settings › Your Petals has Add from a File…, Start from an Example (SHA-256 checksums with Windows' certutil) and Open the Petals Folder. A file gives the petal a name (and an Arabic name), an icon, which files it accepts (extensions, or image, video, audio, pdf, document or any), the program, its arguments with {input}, {output}, {name}, {ext}, {folder} or {inputs}, the result's name, and whether it runs once per file. The petal appears on the Ctrl wheel for files it accepts, even kinds DropWheel doesn't know. DropWheel shows the exact command before the first run and again whenever the file changes, and runs the program directly, never through a shell.
kind:petal.how: Add the file in Settings › Your Petals, then drag matching files, tap Ctrl and drop on its petal.
examples: A petal that runs oxipng on PNG files and saves 'name Optimised.png'.
A petal that saves the checksum of a downloaded ISO to a text file.
A petal that hands videos to HandBrake's command line with your usual settings.
kind:petal.worksOn: The files its 'accepts' list names; one or many.

kind:app.summary: Opens a program, or switches to it when it is already open.
kind:app.details: An app petal is added to a wheel in Settings › Wheels with Add a Petal…, by searching for any app on the PC or choosing 'A program' and a .exe or shortcut (.lnk), with optional Arguments. The petal shows the program's own icon. Choosing it brings the program's window to the front when it is already running (when no arguments are set), and starts it otherwise. If the program has been removed, the petal is dim and says so.
kind:app.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, go to the wheel that has the petal (Tab or the mouse wheel) and choose it.
examples: A Calculator petal on your own wheel to open it from anywhere.
Spotify brought to the front from a wheel instead of hunting for it on the taskbar.
Excel opened with a particular workbook by giving its path as the arguments.

kind:keys.summary: Presses a keyboard shortcut, or a sequence of them, in the app that was in front.
kind:keys.details: A keys petal holds a shortcut such as Ctrl+Shift+T, or several presses in a row (Ctrl+K Ctrl+S); in Settings › Wheels you click the Keys box and press them. The keys go only to the window that was in front when the wheel opened, once it is back in front, and the centre shows them while you rest on the petal. DropWheel's ready-made wheels for browsers, File Explorer, VS Code, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Teams, Zoom, Photoshop, Windows Terminal, Slack and Discord are made of such petals and come first while their app is in front. If that window has closed, a card says the keys weren't pressed.
kind:keys.how: In the app you want, press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose the petal.
examples: Reopen Closed Tab in Chrome from the wheel without remembering Ctrl+Shift+T.
Mute or Raise Hand in Teams or Zoom during a call.
A petal for a VS Code command that needs two shortcuts one after the other.

kind:script.summary: Runs a PowerShell or Command Prompt script, given the clipboard, the selected text or the selected files.
kind:script.details: A script petal is written in Settings › Wheels: choose Runs with (PowerShell or Command Prompt) and Gets (Nothing, The text on the clipboard, The selected text, or The files selected in File Explorer), then type the script. What it gets is in %PETAL_INPUT% ($env:PETAL_INPUT) or the file %PETAL_INPUT_FILE%, and selected files are in %PETAL_FILES%, one per line. It runs hidden; with 'Show what it prints when it finishes' on, a card shows the first line it printed and a click copies all of it, and a script still running after ten minutes is stopped. A script that came in with imported settings is shown to you before it runs the first time.
kind:script.how: Write it in Settings › Wheels › Add a Petal… › Script, then press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose it.
examples: A script that turns the copied title into a web address slug and prints it.
A Command Prompt script that backs up the files selected in File Explorer to a USB drive.
A PowerShell script that shows the PC's IP address on the card.
kind:script.worksOn: Nothing, the clipboard's text, the selected text, or the files selected in File Explorer, as you choose.

kind:folder.summary: Opens a folder in File Explorer.
kind:folder.details: A folder petal is added in Settings › Wheels by choosing Folder and browsing to it; paths such as %USERPROFILE%\Downloads work too. Choosing it opens the folder in File Explorer, and the petal is dim if the folder is no longer there. It is different from the folders on the Alt wheel (Settings › Actions Wheel), which copy or move dropped files into a folder.
kind:folder.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, go to the wheel that has the petal and choose it.
examples: Your Downloads folder opened from the wheel in one move.
A shared office folder opened without clicking through File Explorer.
A Screenshots folder on your own wheel to find the last capture.

kind:link.summary: Opens a web address, or a Windows link such as ms-settings:display.
kind:link.details: A link petal is added in Settings › Wheels by choosing Link and typing an Address: a web page (https://…) or a Windows link such as ms-settings:display. Choosing it opens the page in your usual browser, or the page of Windows Settings the link names. The petal shows a globe unless you pick another icon.
kind:link.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, go to the wheel that has the petal and choose it.
examples: Your webmail or school portal opened from the wheel.
ms-settings:display to change the screen's scaling quickly.
ms-settings:bluetooth to pair headphones without searching through Settings.

kind:group.summary: Holds petals of its own that fly out around it as glass bubbles, such as More.
kind:group.details: A group petal opens its petals on an orbit of glass bubbles just outside the ring, turned away from the screen's edge, while the rest of the ring steps back. Point at it, click it, or hold over it while dragging, then choose a bubble; the arrow keys, Enter and 1 to 9 work on the bubbles, and Esc, the group again or the centre takes them back in. Your own groups hold up to eight petals and are made in Settings › Wheels; DropWheel's own More groups hold the extra petals of the Quick and Arrange wheels, of the tools wheel when it has more than twelve, and the actions not placed on the actions wheel.
kind:group.how: Rest on or click the group petal (for example MORE), then choose one of its bubbles.
examples: MORE on the Alt wheel to reach Copy Path, Copy Name, VS Code and Terminal.
The Case group on the Text wheel with UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title and Sentence case.
Your own 'Office' group with petals for Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

kind:windows.summary: Shows the windows that are open as petals, to switch to one.
kind:windows.details: The Open Windows petal (WINDOWS on the wheel) opens around itself with a bubble for each open window, showing its app's icon, with the window's title in the centre. Choosing one brings that window to the front, and a card says so if it has closed in the meantime. When no other windows are open the petal is dim; add it to any wheel in Settings › Wheels with 'Open windows'.
kind:windows.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose WINDOWS on a wheel that has it, and pick the window.
examples: Jump back to a browser window buried under ten others.
Switch between two Excel workbooks without Alt+Tab.
Find a small chat window hidden behind a full-screen video.

kind:clips.summary: Shows the last things you copied as petals that paste them into the app in front.
kind:clips.details: The Recent Clips petal (CLIPS) shows the last eight clips, pinned ones first: text, pictures or files, each a petal that pastes it where you are working; on the Clipboard wheel the clips sit right on the ring. If a clip can't be pasted it stays on the clipboard for Ctrl+V. It comes from DropWheel's clipboard history (search, pin, delete), whose switches are in Settings › Screen & Text; private copies such as passwords are never kept, and the history is remembered after DropWheel closes only if you ask. When nothing has been copied yet the petal is dim.
kind:clips.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, go to the Clipboard wheel and choose a clip.
examples: Paste an address you copied an hour ago without finding it again.
Put three copied lines into a form one after another.
Paste a screenshot you copied earlier into a chat.

kind:workspaces.summary: Opens a saved set of apps and puts every window back in its place.
kind:workspaces.details: A workspace keeps the apps open now and where their windows are, under a name such as Work or Study; Save Workspace (SAVE LAYOUT) lets you name it and tick which windows to keep. The WORKSPACES petal on the Work wheel opens around itself with every saved workspace (each showing its first app's icon) and Save Workspace, and a single workspace can also be a petal of its own. Choosing one starts the apps that aren't running and puts every window back in its place, maximised ones maximised.
kind:workspaces.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, go to the Work wheel, choose WORKSPACES and pick one.
examples: A 'Work' workspace that opens Outlook, Teams and Excel side by side every morning.
A 'Study' set with the browser on the left and Word on the right.
An 'Editing' layout with Premiere on one screen and File Explorer on the other.

do:system.darkmode.summary: Switches Windows and your apps between light and dark mode with one petal.
do:system.darkmode.details: Dark Mode changes the same two switches as Windows Settings for colours: the mode for apps and the mode for Windows itself, together. DropWheel tells every open window that the setting changed, as Settings does, so apps that follow the Windows theme change at once. The petal shows whether dark mode is on now, read from Windows, so it is right even if you changed it somewhere else. Choose it again to go back to light.
do:system.darkmode.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose DARK MODE on the Quick wheel. You can also type 'dark mode' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: Working late at night: choose DARK MODE and File Explorer, Settings and the taskbar turn dark.
Showing slides on a projector in a bright room: switch back to light so text is easier to read.
Reading in bed on a laptop: one petal makes the screen easier on your eyes.

do:system.mute.summary: Mutes or unmutes the PC's speakers or headphones in one step.
do:system.mute.details: Mute Sound turns the sound of the default speakers or headphones off, or back on, like the speaker button in the taskbar. The petal shows whether the sound is muted now. If Windows finds no speakers, the petal is dimmed and says No speakers found. Volume Up on the Media wheel also unmutes the sound.
do:system.mute.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose MUTE on the Quick wheel; it is on the Media wheel too.
examples: A video starts playing loudly in a quiet office: MUTE silences the PC at once.
Your phone rings while music plays on the laptop: mute, take the call, then unmute.
In a library, mute the laptop before opening a YouTube link a friend sent.

do:system.mic.summary: Mutes or unmutes the microphone for every app at once.
do:system.mic.details: Mute Microphone mutes the default microphone in Windows itself, so Teams, Zoom, Discord, the browser and every other app hear nothing. Choose it again to unmute. The petal shows whether the microphone is muted now. If no microphone is found, the petal is dimmed and says No microphone found.
do:system.mic.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose MIC on the Quick wheel.
examples: Someone walks in during a Zoom meeting: MIC mutes you even if Zoom is hidden behind other windows.
You are not sure whether a website is listening: mute the microphone for all apps.
Coughing during a Discord voice chat: mute, cough, unmute.

do:system.awake.summary: Keeps the PC and the screen from going to sleep until you turn it off.
do:system.awake.details: Keep Awake asks Windows to keep both the PC and the display on, so the sleep and screen-off timers don't kick in. It stays on until you choose the petal again or DropWheel quits. The petal shows whether it is on. Your power settings are not changed; turning it off lets the normal timers work again.
do:system.awake.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose AWAKE on the Quick wheel.
examples: Downloading a 20 GB game overnight: AWAKE stops the PC from sleeping halfway.
Following a recipe on the kitchen laptop: the screen stays on while your hands are busy.
Showing a PDF to a client: the screen won't go dark while you talk.

do:system.lock.summary: Locks the PC at once, so it asks for your password or PIN to get back in.
do:system.lock.details: Lock does the same as Win+L. Your apps stay open and nothing is closed or saved; the sign-in screen shows until you sign in again. Use it whenever you step away from the PC.
do:system.lock.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose LOCK on the Quick wheel.
examples: Going for coffee at the office: LOCK keeps colleagues away from your open e-mail.
Doing online banking with children in the house: lock the PC before you leave the room.
Answering the door in a shared flat: lock first so your documents stay private.

do:system.sleep.summary: Puts the PC to sleep straight away.
do:system.sleep.details: Sleep does what Sleep in the Start menu's power button does: the PC goes into its low-power sleep and your open apps stay where they were. Wake it as usual for your PC, with a key, the mouse or the power button. Save important work first, as with any sleep.
do:system.sleep.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose SLEEP.
examples: Done for the day at your desk: SLEEP, and the PC is ready in seconds tomorrow.
Leaving for a meeting with the laptop: put it to sleep to save battery.
A film in the browser has finished late at night: sleep the PC without looking for the Start menu.

do:system.hidden.summary: Shows or hides hidden files and folders in File Explorer.
do:system.hidden.details: Hidden Files flips File Explorer's setting for showing hidden items. Open File Explorer windows and the desktop refresh at once, so hidden files appear or disappear without reopening anything. The petal shows whether hidden files are shown now. Protected Windows system files stay hidden either way.
do:system.hidden.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose HIDDEN on the Quick wheel; it is also on the File Explorer wheel, which comes first while File Explorer is in front.
examples: Looking for the AppData folder to back up a game save: show hidden files, then hide them again.
A USB stick says it is full but looks empty: show hidden items to see what is on it.
Copying a .env settings file from a project folder: make hidden files visible first.

do:system.extensions.summary: Shows or hides file name extensions such as .jpg and .pdf in File Explorer.
do:system.extensions.details: File Extensions flips File Explorer's setting for file name extensions. With it on, 'photo' shows as 'photo.jpg', so you can tell a picture from a PDF or change a file's type when renaming. File Explorer windows and the desktop refresh straight away. The petal shows whether extensions are shown now.
do:system.extensions.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose FILE TYPES on the Quick wheel; it is also on the File Explorer wheel.
examples: Two files in Downloads are both called 'report': show extensions to see which is .docx and which is .pdf.
A website asks for a .png and you are not sure what your picture is: turn extensions on and check.
An e-mail attachment called invoice.pdf looks odd: extensions show if it is really invoice.pdf.exe.

do:system.desktopicons.summary: Shows or hides all the icons on the desktop.
do:system.desktopicons.details: Desktop Icons does what the desktop's own right-click menu does with View, Show desktop icons. The files stay where they are; only the icons are hidden. The petal reads the desktop itself to show whether icons are visible now. Choose it again to bring them back.
do:system.desktopicons.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose DESKTOP ICONS on the Quick wheel.
examples: Sharing your screen in a Teams call: hide the cluttered desktop icons first.
Taking a screenshot of a new wallpaper with no icons in the way.
Recording a tutorial video: a clean desktop looks tidier.

do:system.recyclebin.summary: Empties the Recycle Bin on every drive, after Windows asks you to confirm.
do:system.recyclebin.details: Empty Recycle Bin removes everything in the Recycle Bin on all drives and frees the space it takes. Windows shows its usual question first, so nothing is deleted unless you agree. This can't be undone: files emptied from the bin are gone.
do:system.recyclebin.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose EMPTY BIN on the Quick wheel, then confirm in the Windows dialog.
examples: Drive C is almost full after you deleted old videos: empty the bin to actually get the space back.
A monthly tidy-up: empty the bin from the wheel instead of looking for its icon on the desktop.
Windows warns about low disk space before an update: emptying the bin is the quickest first step.

do:system.eject.summary: Safely removes every USB drive, memory card and disc in one go.
do:system.eject.details: Eject Drives locks each removable drive, and each disc drive with a disc in it, takes it offline and ejects it, like Safely Remove Hardware does. A card then says Safe to remove with the drive letters, such as E: F:. If a file on a drive is still open, that drive is left alone and the card says Some drives are in use, with its letter. When nothing removable is plugged in, the petal is dimmed and says No USB drives or discs.
do:system.eject.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose EJECT.
examples: You finished copying photos to a USB stick: eject it so the files aren't damaged when you pull it out.
A camera's SD card is in the laptop: eject it safely before putting it back in the camera.
A DVD is in the drive: EJECT releases it and opens the tray.

do:system.clearclipboard.summary: Empties the Windows clipboard so what you copied can no longer be pasted.
do:system.clearclipboard.details: Empty Clipboard forgets whatever is copied right now: text, a picture or files. A card confirms Clipboard emptied. It doesn't touch DropWheel's clipboard history; Clear Clipboard History on the wheels does that. Use it after copying a password or other private details.
do:system.clearclipboard.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose CLEAR.
examples: You copied a password from your password manager: clear the clipboard so it can't be pasted by accident.
Before lending your laptop: forget the private message you just copied.
Word keeps pasting an old picture: empty the clipboard and copy again.

do:system.showdesktop.summary: Hides every window to show the desktop, then brings them all back.
do:system.showdesktop.details: Show Desktop does what Win+D does: all windows go down at once so you can reach the desktop. Choose it again and the same windows come back as they were. Nothing is closed.
do:system.showdesktop.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose SHOW DESKTOP.
examples: You need a file saved on the desktop but ten windows cover it: show the desktop, then bring them back.
Someone walks up to your screen: hide every window at once.
Checking a sticky note or widget on the desktop in the middle of work.

do:system.taskview.summary: Opens Windows Task View to see every open window and your desktops.
do:system.taskview.details: Task View shows all open windows as large previews, the same as Win+Tab. Click one to switch to it. It also shows your virtual desktops, so you can move between them or add one.
do:system.taskview.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose TASK VIEW.
examples: Twenty browser and Word windows open: Task View shows them all so you can pick the right one.
Keep work and personal apps on two desktops and switch between them.
Find a small window that slipped behind everything else.

do:system.notifications.details: Notifications opens Windows' own notification centre, where messages from apps that you missed are kept. Read them there, click one to open its app, or clear them. It is the same panel the taskbar opens.
do:system.notifications.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose NOTIFY.
examples: A message popped up while you were typing and vanished: open the notifications to read it.
Check whether an Outlook meeting reminder came in while you were away.
Clear a long list of old app alerts in one place.

do:system.bluetooth.details: Bluetooth switches the PC's Bluetooth radio, like the Bluetooth button in Windows' quick settings. The petal shows whether it is on. If Windows refuses the change, a card says Windows didn't allow the change. On a PC without Bluetooth the petal is dimmed and says No Bluetooth on this PC.
do:system.bluetooth.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose BLUETOOTH.
examples: Connect your wireless earbuds: turn Bluetooth on first.
On a plane or to save laptop battery: switch Bluetooth off.
A Bluetooth mouse acts strangely: turn Bluetooth off and on again.

do:system.settings.details: Windows Settings opens the Settings app at its home page, the same as Win+I. From there you can change the display, sound, network, apps and everything else Windows offers. It is not on any wheel at first: add it to one of your wheels in DropWheel Settings under Wheels, or find it in the command palette.
do:system.settings.how: Press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'windows settings' and press Enter, or add the SETTINGS petal to a wheel in DropWheel Settings under Wheels.
examples: Change the screen resolution for a projector: open Windows Settings and go to Display.
Connect to a new Wi-Fi network at a hotel.
Uninstall an app you no longer use from the Apps page.

do:screen.circle.summary: Circle anything on the screen (a sentence, a number, a date, a picture, a QR code) and the wheel opens with what can be done with it, all on this PC.
do:screen.circle.details: Press Ctrl+Win+C and the screen stands still, with a glowing edge. Circle anything, scribble over a word, run a line along a sentence, or click a paragraph or a picture: the pointer lights up the paragraph a click would take. DropWheel reads what you took (with the text recognition built into Windows; QR codes and barcodes too) and the wheel opens on it. For words: COPY TEXT, TRANSLATE (the translation is laid over the original, paragraph by paragraph, in its own colours, with Original to compare), EXPLAIN, ASK (a question box that keeps the conversation going), SUMMARY, SEARCH, READ ALOUD, and TABLE or EXCEL when the words stand in rows and columns. What the text holds comes first: OPEN LINK, EMAIL, CALL, CALENDAR for a date (an event file any calendar opens), YOUR TIME for a time given in another zone, CONVERT for units (kilometres and miles, kilos and pounds, °C and °F, feet and inches, feddans), CURRENCY at today's rates, RESULT for a sum, COLOUR for a colour code. For a picture: DESCRIBE, ASK, COPY PICTURE, SAVE, CUT OUT (the subject, with see-through edges), PIN, COLOURS, and TOOLS for every conversion. The middle of the wheel already shows the answer when there is one: a conversion, a sum, the time where you are. Explaining, asking and describing use the AI models on this PC, downloaded once; only CURRENCY goes online, and only when you choose it, to fetch today's rates. Esc or a right-click puts the screen back.
do:screen.circle.how: Press Ctrl+Win+C (or press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose CIRCLE on the Screen wheel), circle what you want, then choose a petal. The shortcut can be changed in Settings › Screen & Text.
examples: Circle a price in dollars to see it in your own currency at today's rate.
Circle a paragraph in another language and read it translated in place, over the original.
Circle a meeting time given in another time zone and add it to your calendar in your own time.

do:screen.area.summary: Takes a screenshot of the part of the screen you drag over, then opens the conversion wheel on it.
do:screen.area.details: The screen under the pointer freezes and you drag a box over the part you want; its size in pixels shows as you drag, and Esc or a right-click cancels. The picture is saved as a PNG named like 'Screenshot 2026-10-21 16.40.05.png' in the Screenshots folder inside Pictures, and copied to the clipboard so you can paste it anywhere. A card says Screenshot saved and copied and shows where it went, with Show in Folder and Open. The conversion wheel then opens on the picture, to turn it into a JPG, a PDF or a smaller file, or to use a tool on it.
do:screen.area.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose SNIP on the Quick or Screen wheel and drag over the area; Take a Screenshot in the tray menu does the same.
examples: Send part of a web page in WhatsApp: snip it, then press Ctrl+V in the chat.
An error message for IT support: snip it and attach the PNG from the Screenshots folder.
Need an order confirmation as a PDF: snip it and choose PDF on the wheel that opens.

do:screen.full.summary: Takes a screenshot of the whole screen under the pointer and opens the conversion wheel on it.
do:screen.full.details: Screenshot the Screen captures the monitor the pointer is on, at its full resolution, with no area to choose. Like the other screenshots it is saved as a PNG in the Screenshots folder inside Pictures and copied to the clipboard. A card shows where it went, with Show in Folder and Open. The conversion wheel then opens on the picture at the pointer.
do:screen.full.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose SCREEN on the Screen wheel, or open MORE on the Quick wheel and choose SCREEN.
examples: Capture a whole video call layout to share with your team.
On two monitors, point at the right one and capture only that screen.
Save a full-screen game moment, then compress it on the wheel to post online.

do:screen.record.summary: Records an area or the whole screen to an MP4 video, with the PC's sound and your microphone if you want.
do:screen.record.details: Drag over the area to record, or press Enter for the whole screen; a bar appears with Record and switches for the PC's sound (on at first), the microphone, showing clicks and shortcuts, your camera in a round bubble, and Polish (on at first: zooms in on clicks, a smooth pointer and a coloured background). Record counts 3, 2, 1, then the bar shows the time with Stop and save and Cancel; choosing the petal again, which now reads STOP, also stops. The video is saved as 'Recording 2026-10-21 16.40.05.mp4' in the Screen Recordings folder inside Videos, and a card shows where with Show in Folder and Open. The conversion wheel then opens on it, to make a GIF, a smaller file or a shorter clip. The red frame and the bar stay out of the video. Recording needs FFmpeg; without it a card says FFmpeg was not found.
do:screen.record.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose RECORD on the Screen wheel (or Record the Screen in the tray menu), drag over the area and press Record.
examples: Show your mother how to book a doctor's appointment online: record the browser with your voice and send the MP4.
An app keeps crashing: record it happening and attach the video to your report.
Turn a 10-second chart animation into a GIF: record it, then choose GIF on the wheel that opens.

do:screen.scroll.summary: Takes one tall screenshot of a whole long page: DropWheel scrolls it and joins what it sees.
do:screen.scroll.details: Drag over the part of the window that scrolls, such as a web page or a chat; DropWheel puts the pointer there, scrolls down by itself and joins each new piece into one picture, with sticky headers and footers shown once. It stops at the end of the page, when you press Esc or when you move the mouse, and the picture can be up to 30,000 pixels tall. If the page changes while scrolling, the part so far is kept and the card says so. The picture is saved in the Screenshots folder inside Pictures and copied to the clipboard, a card shows where with Show in Folder and Open, and the conversion wheel opens on it.
do:screen.scroll.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose SCROLL SHOT on the Screen wheel, then drag over the scrolling part of the window.
examples: Keep a long online receipt as one picture, then turn it into a PDF on the wheel.
Save a long WhatsApp Web conversation as a single image instead of ten screenshots.
Send a colleague a whole web page design to comment on.

do:screen.text.summary: Copies the words from any part of the screen, even in pictures and videos, and reads QR codes too.
do:screen.text.details: Drag over the text; the Text from the Screen window shows a preview and the words found, which you can change before pressing Copy Text. Buttons let you Translate between Arabic and English on this PC (the translation model downloads once), Fix Keyboard Layout, Join Lines broken by the screen, Search the Web, Copy as Table to paste into Excel cell by cell, or Save as Excel, which saves the table in Documents and opens it. QR codes and barcodes in the area are listed with Copy, plus Open Link for web addresses. Reading uses the text recognition built into Windows, so a Windows language that can read text must be installed; if none is, the window says how to add one under Settings › Time & language › Language.
do:screen.text.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose COPY TEXT on the Screen wheel (or Text from the Screen in the tray menu), then drag over the words.
examples: Copy a phone number shown in a YouTube video without typing it.
A price table in a picture that won't let you select text: Copy as Table and paste it into Excel.
A QR code on a web page: drag over it to read it and open its link.

do:screen.pin.summary: Keeps a piece of the screen floating on top of every window, to compare or copy from.
do:screen.pin.details: Drag over an area and it stays exactly there as a floating picture above all windows; drag it anywhere you like. The mouse wheel makes it bigger or smaller (20% to 400%), Ctrl with the mouse wheel makes it see-through, and Ctrl+C copies it. A right-click offers Copy, Save to Screenshots, Open the Wheel for It, Actual Size, See Through, Close and Close All Pinned. Esc or a double-click puts it away, and you can pin several at once.
do:screen.pin.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose PIN on the Screen wheel and drag over the part to keep.
examples: Typing numbers from a bank statement into a form: pin the statement beside the form.
Comparing two prices in different browser tabs: pin one, then switch to the other.
Following a recipe photo while writing a shopping list in Notepad.

do:screen.live.summary: Keeps part of another window live and on top of everything, changing as it changes there.
do:screen.live.details: Drag over part of an app's window, such as a video call, a stream or a progress bar, and a small window shows that part live above all others. Windows draws it, so nothing is copied or recorded and it costs almost nothing. You can resize it and it keeps its shape; its top bar shows the window's name with See-through (three steps) and Close, and Esc also closes it. It closes by itself when the source window closes. Up to 6 live regions can be open, and the desktop and taskbar can't be used.
do:screen.live.how: It is not on a wheel at first: press Ctrl+Win+K and type 'live region', or add LIVE to a wheel in DropWheel Settings under Wheels, then drag over part of a window.
examples: Keep the score corner of a football stream in view while you work in Excel.
Keep the speaker's video from a Zoom call visible while you take notes in Word.
Watch the progress bar of a long export in another app without switching to it.

do:screen.private.summary: Takes a screenshot with e-mail addresses, phone numbers, card numbers and passwords already covered, to share safely.
do:screen.private.details: Drag over an area; the picture waits in DropWheel's temporary folder and opens in the Redact Photo window, which looks for private details straight away and covers each one with a box: e-mail addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, IBANs, IP addresses and passwords. You can also press Faces or Text to cover those, drag on the picture to cover any other area, move or resize a box, or remove it with Delete. Style can be Solid, in a colour you choose, or Blur. Save Redacted Copy saves only the covered copy, named like 'Screenshot 2026-10-21 16.40.05 Redacted.png', in the Screenshots folder inside Pictures, puts it on the clipboard and shows where it is; the uncovered picture is deleted, and closing the window without saving keeps nothing.
do:screen.private.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose PRIVATE SHOT on the Screen wheel, drag over the area, check the boxes and press Save Redacted Copy.
examples: Show customer support your order page without your e-mail address and card number.
Post a screenshot of a bug on a public forum without your login details.
Send a bank transfer confirmation to a landlord with your IBAN covered.

do:screen.colour.summary: Picks the colour of any pixel on the screen and copies it as HEX, with RGB, HSL and contrast.
do:screen.colour.details: The screen freezes and a round magnifier shows the pixels around the pointer with the colour's HEX code and RGB numbers; the arrow keys move one pixel, or 10 with Shift. A click, Enter or Space picks the colour, copies its HEX code (like #3B82F6) and opens a Colour card with HEX, RGB, HSL and WPF / C# values, each with a copy button. If you picked a colour before, the card shows the two together with their contrast ratio and a verdict such as Easy to read (AA). Pick Another starts again, and Esc or a right-click cancels.
do:screen.colour.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, choose COLOUR on the Screen wheel, point at the colour and click.
examples: Match the blue of your company logo on its website for a PowerPoint slide.
Check whether grey text on a white button is readable: pick both colours and read the contrast.
Find the exact colour of a sofa in an online photo to look for matching cushions.

do:screen.ruler.summary: Measures distances and sizes on the screen in pixels.
do:screen.ruler.details: The screen freezes and the ruler starts in Spacing mode: point between edges and it finds where the colour changes up, down, left and right, showing width × height in pixels. Tab switches to Box mode, where you drag a box and see its width, height and diagonal. A click, or Ctrl+C, copies the size, like 120 × 48. Esc or a right-click closes it.
do:screen.ruler.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose RULER on the Screen wheel.
examples: Check that a banner on your shop's website is exactly 728 pixels wide.
Measure the gap between two buttons in a design before telling the developer.
Find how big a photo appears on a page so you can make yours the same size.

do:draw.screen.summary: Lets you draw with pen, highlighter, arrows, boxes and text over anything on the screen.
do:draw.screen.details: A drawing layer covers the monitor under the pointer, with a strip at the top: Pen (P), Highlighter (H), Line (L), Arrow (A), Box (R), Ring (O), Text (T) and Eraser (E), eight colours, three sizes (1, 2, 3), Undo, Redo and Clear all. You can draw over the live screen, over a still of it (F), on a Whiteboard (W) or a Blackboard (K), and Let clicks through keeps the drawing while you use the apps under it. Shift keeps lines at 45° steps and boxes and rings round, and Ctrl with the mouse wheel changes the size. Save (Ctrl+S) saves 'Drawing 2026-10-21 16.40.05.png' in the Screenshots folder inside Pictures with a card that opens the wheel for it, and Copy (Ctrl+C) copies the screen with your drawing. Esc puts it away, and so does choosing DRAW again.
do:draw.screen.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose DRAW; Draw on Screen in the tray menu does the same.
examples: Circle a button with a red ring while sharing your screen in Teams.
Highlight the total on a spreadsheet and save it as a picture for your manager.
Show a child where to click on a school website with arrows.

do:draw.whiteboard.summary: Covers the screen with a clean white board to draw and explain on.
do:draw.whiteboard.details: Whiteboard opens the same drawing layer as Draw on Screen, with a white board over the monitor under the pointer. All the drawing tools, colours, sizes, undo, save and copy work the same, and white ink switches to black so it shows. Press W to go back to the screen and W again for the board, or K for the blackboard; Esc puts it away. If a drawing is already open, the petal switches it to the white board.
do:draw.whiteboard.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose WHITE BOARD.
examples: Explain a maths problem to a student in an online lesson.
Sketch a kitchen layout during a video call with a builder.
Brainstorm ideas in a meeting and save the board as a PNG with Ctrl+S.

do:draw.blackboard.summary: Covers the screen with a dark board to draw on in white and colour.
do:draw.blackboard.details: Blackboard opens the same drawing layer as Draw on Screen, with a dark green-black board over the monitor under the pointer. All the drawing tools, colours, sizes, undo, save and copy work the same, and black ink switches to white so it shows. Press K to go back to the screen and K again for the board, or W for the whiteboard; Esc puts it away. If a drawing is already open, the petal switches it to the blackboard.
do:draw.blackboard.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose BLACK BOARD.
examples: Teach a chemistry lesson online the way you would on a classroom board.
Draw a quick diagram in white during an evening call, when a bright white board would glare.
Write the steps of a recipe in colour for a live cooking stream.

do:draw.zoom.summary: Zooms into the screen with the mouse wheel, and lets you draw on what is zoomed.
do:draw.zoom.details: Zoom In freezes the monitor under the pointer and zooms straight to 2× around the pointer. The mouse wheel, or + and -, zooms from 1× to 8×, moving the pointer moves around the picture, and 0 goes back to 1×. A click or D opens the drawing tools over the zoomed view, and Ctrl+C copies what is shown. Esc or a right-click goes back. The picture is a still, so a video under it does not move while zoomed.
do:draw.zoom.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose ZOOM.
examples: Show the small print of a contract clearly during a screen share.
Zoom into an Excel formula while teaching a class, then circle the mistake.
Point out a tiny icon in a settings window to someone on a call.

do:draw.lens.summary: Shows a round magnifying glass that follows the pointer over everything.
do:draw.lens.details: Magnifier shows a live circle that enlarges whatever is under the pointer as you move, starting at 2.5×. Ctrl and the mouse wheel change how much, from 1.25× to 12×, and the level shows at the bottom of the glass. Clicks pass through it so you can keep working, and it stays out of screenshots and recordings. Esc or choosing MAGNIFIER again puts it away.
do:draw.lens.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose MAGNIFIER.
examples: Read the tiny print on a scanned letter without zooming the whole page.
Help an older parent see small menu items while they use the PC.
Check a photo's sharpness up close before printing it.

do:draw.spotlight.summary: Darkens the screen except a soft circle around the pointer, to show people where to look.
do:draw.spotlight.details: Spotlight dims every screen and leaves a bright circle that follows the pointer; monitors without the pointer stay dark. Clicks pass through to the apps, so you can keep working. Ctrl and the mouse wheel make the circle bigger or smaller. Esc or choosing SPOTLIGHT again turns it off.
do:draw.spotlight.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose SPOTLIGHT.
examples: Walking a team through a busy dashboard in a meeting: the light shows the number you mean.
Recording a tutorial where viewers must follow the mouse.
Teaching a class on a projector: students know where to look on a crowded page.

do:draw.clicks.summary: Shows rings where you click and the shortcuts you press, for recordings and presentations.
do:draw.clicks.details: Show Clicks and Keys draws a ring at each click: amber for the left button, blue for the right and green for the middle. Shortcuts with Ctrl, Alt or Win, and keys such as F5 or Esc, appear in pills at the bottom of the screen, like Ctrl + C. Plain typing is not shown unless you turn on Show every key in DropWheel Settings under Screen & Text, so passwords never appear by default. Clicks pass through, and choosing SHOW CLICKS again turns it off.
do:draw.clicks.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected, press Tab until the Draw & Present wheel shows and choose SHOW CLICKS.
examples: Recording an Excel tutorial: viewers see each click and every Ctrl+C you press.
Training new staff over Teams: they can follow which button you clicked.
Showing a parent a keyboard shortcut: the keys appear on screen as you press them.

do:draw.timer.summary: Shows a countdown timer or a stopwatch on top of everything, big enough for a room.
do:draw.timer.details: The Timer opens in the bottom-right corner with presets of 1, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 25 min, a box for any time such as 7, 1:30, 90s or 1h 15m, and Stopwatch. While it runs you get Pause (or Space), A minute more, Start again, Bigger or smaller, Another time and Close, and you can drag it anywhere. At the end the digits flash red, three soft bell notes chime and a card says Time's up. The time left also shows in the middle of the wheel. Esc or choosing TIMER again closes it.
do:draw.timer.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose TIMER on the Draw & Present wheel or the Work wheel; Timer in the tray menu does the same.
examples: A 25-minute study block for homework, with a chime at the end.
Give students 10 minutes for a quiz, shown large on the classroom projector.
Time each speaker's 3 minutes in a meeting.

do:media.playpause.summary: Plays or pauses whatever is playing in any app, such as Spotify, YouTube in a browser or Media Player.
do:media.playpause.details: Play or Pause controls the music or video that Windows shows in its own media controls, even when the player is hidden behind other windows. Its label changes between PLAY and PAUSE, and the middle of the wheel says Playing or Paused. When nothing is playing, the petal is dimmed and says Nothing is playing.
do:media.playpause.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose PLAY on the Media wheel.
examples: Someone talks to you while Spotify plays: pause it without finding the Spotify window.
A YouTube lesson in a background browser tab: pause it while you take notes in Word.
Resume a podcast after a phone call.

do:media.next.summary: Skips to the next track in the app that is playing.
do:media.next.details: Next skips to the next song or video in whatever app shows in Windows' media controls, such as Spotify or a browser. It works without switching to the player. When nothing is playing, the petal is dimmed and says Nothing is playing.
do:media.next.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose NEXT on the Media wheel.
examples: A song you don't like comes on in Spotify while you are writing an e-mail: skip it.
Move to the next video in a YouTube playlist without leaving your spreadsheet.
Skip an episode intro in a podcast app.

do:media.previous.summary: Goes back to the previous track in the app that is playing.
do:media.previous.details: Previous goes back to the previous song or video in whatever app shows in Windows' media controls. Many players restart the current track first if it has been playing a while; that is up to the player. When nothing is playing, the petal is dimmed and says Nothing is playing.
do:media.previous.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose PREVIOUS on the Media wheel.
examples: You skipped a song by mistake in Spotify: go back to it.
Hear the last lesson video in a playlist again.
Replay a track you liked while cooking with the laptop on the counter.

do:media.shuffle.summary: Turns shuffle on or off in the music player, if it has shuffle.
do:media.shuffle.details: Shuffle switches the player's shuffle on or off through Windows' media controls. The petal shows whether shuffle is on. If the player has no shuffle, the petal is dimmed and says This player can't shuffle; if nothing is playing it says Nothing is playing.
do:media.shuffle.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose SHUFFLE on the Media wheel.
examples: Your Spotify playlist always starts with the same songs: turn shuffle on.
Listening to an album in order: turn shuffle off.
Mix up a long party playlist without opening the player.

do:media.repeat.summary: Changes the player's repeat between repeat all, repeat one and off, if it has repeat.
do:media.repeat.details: Repeat steps through the player's repeat modes each time you choose it: off, then repeat all, then repeat one, then off again. The petal shows whether repeat is on. If the player has no repeat, the petal is dimmed and says This player can't repeat; if nothing is playing it says Nothing is playing.
do:media.repeat.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose REPEAT on the Media wheel.
examples: Learning a song on guitar: set repeat one to hear it again and again.
Keep a relaxing playlist going all evening with repeat all.
Turn repeat off so the album stops at the end.

do:media.volumeup.summary: Turns the volume up one step, and unmutes the sound if it was muted.
do:media.volumeup.details: Volume Up raises the default speakers' volume by one step of the Windows volume slider. If the sound was muted, it is unmuted first. A card shows the new level, such as Volume 64%. If no speakers are found, the petal is dimmed and says No speakers found.
do:media.volumeup.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose LOUDER on the Media wheel.
examples: A quiet speaker in a Teams call: turn it up a few steps without finding the volume icon.
Your laptop has no volume keys: use the wheel instead.
A film is too quiet in a noisy room: choose LOUDER a few times.

do:media.volumedown.summary: Turns the volume down one step.
do:media.volumedown.details: Volume Down lowers the default speakers' volume by one step of the Windows volume slider. A card shows the new level, such as Volume 40%. If no speakers are found, the petal is dimmed and says No speakers found.
do:media.volumedown.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose QUIETER on the Media wheel.
examples: An advert suddenly blasts in a browser tab: turn it down a few steps.
Late at night, lower the music so you don't wake anyone.
A colleague's voice is too loud in your headphones during a call.

do:petal.palette.summary: Opens a search box where you type what you want: any action, a petal for selected files, an app, a file or a sum.
do:petal.palette.details: The Command Palette opens over the window in front and finds things as you type, in English or Arabic: every action of every wheel, each wheel itself, every petal for the files selected in File Explorer, DropWheel's windows, the apps on the PC, what you copied lately, files found by Search by Meaning, snippets and workspaces. Type a sum or unit conversion such as 12% of 340 or 5 km in mi and Enter copies the answer. Use the arrow keys to choose, Enter to run, Ctrl+Enter for the other action (such as opening a file's folder) and Esc to close. The microphone button lets you say a command instead. If nothing fits, it offers to search the web.
do:petal.palette.how: Press Ctrl+Win+K, choose COMMANDS on the Work wheel, or choose Command Palette in the tray menu.
examples: Type 'rec' and press Enter to start Record the Screen without looking for its wheel.
Select 5 photos in File Explorer, press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'pdf' and press Enter to make one PDF.
Type '15% of 2400' to get the answer copied for an invoice.
do:petal.palette.worksOn: Files selected in File Explorer, if any, to offer their petals; otherwise nothing.

do:petal.clipboard.summary: Opens the wheel for what you copied: files, a screenshot or text; a copied link becomes a QR code.
do:petal.clipboard.details: Clipboard's Wheel looks at the clipboard: copied files open the conversion wheel for them, or the actions wheel if a folder is among them. A copied picture is saved as 'Clipboard 2026-10-21 16.40.05.png' in the Screenshots folder inside Pictures, and copied text as a .txt file in the DropWheel folder inside Documents, and the conversion wheel opens on that file. A single copied link (a web address, mailto or tel) opens Create QR Code with the link filled in. When the clipboard is empty, the petal is dimmed and says The clipboard is empty.
do:petal.clipboard.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z with nothing selected and choose CLIPBOARD on the Quick wheel or the Clipboard wheel.
examples: You copied a picture from a web page: open the clipboard's wheel and save it as a JPG.
You copied a paragraph from an e-mail: turn it into a PDF on the wheel.
You copied your shop's website address: get a QR code to print on a flyer.
do:petal.clipboard.worksOn: What is on the clipboard: copied files or folders, a picture, text or a link.

do:petal.history.summary: Shows what DropWheel made lately, so you can find a result or undo it.
do:petal.history.details: DropWheel History lists finished conversions and tools, newest first, each with when it happened and the result's name. Show in File Explorer opens the folder with the result selected. Undo moves the results to the Recycle Bin, puts the old names back after a rename, or puts files back from the Recycle Bin. Clear History empties the list. The history stays on this PC, and if keeping a history is off in Settings, the window says so.
do:petal.history.how: It is not on a wheel at first: choose History in the tray menu or in DropWheel Settings, or type 'history' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: You compressed a video yesterday and can't find it: open History and choose Show in File Explorer.
You converted 30 photos to the wrong format: Undo sends the results to the Recycle Bin.
You renamed a folder of files by mistake: Undo puts the old names back.

do:petal.search.summary: Finds files by what they are about: the words in them, their name, or what a photo or video shows.
do:petal.search.details: Search by Meaning lets you type things like 'receipt from the pharmacy' or 'beach photos' and finds matching files in your Pictures, Documents, Desktop, Downloads and Videos folders. It is off until you press Turn On; then DropWheel reads those folders while the PC is idle and keeps the index on this PC. Finding photos and videos by what they show needs DropWheel's picture models, downloaded once. Enter opens the first result, and you can drag any result into another app. When you type a question, Ask Your Files answers from what your documents say, with the files it came from; this needs the AI model, downloaded once.
do:petal.search.how: It is not on a wheel at first: choose Search by Meaning in the tray menu, or type 'search' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: You can't remember what you named a scanned electricity bill: type 'electricity bill' and it shows up.
Find holiday photos of the sea without knowing which folder they are in.
Ask 'when does my car insurance end?' and get the answer from the policy PDF.

do:petal.scan.summary: Scans paper pages with your phone's camera into one searchable PDF on the PC.
do:petal.scan.details: Scan with Phone shows a QR code; scan it with the phone's camera to open a camera page in the phone's browser, over your Wi-Fi with nothing going through the internet. Photograph each page or Choose photos, drag the corners if needed, pick Document, Colour, Grey or Black & white, and press Save as PDF. DropWheel finds each page, straightens it on the PC and saves one searchable PDF in the Scans folder inside Documents, or a folder you pick with Choose. The phone and the PC must be on the same network, and Windows may ask you to allow DropWheel on private networks. Sharing stops when the window closes, or after 20 minutes with no activity.
do:petal.scan.how: It is not on a wheel at first: choose Scan with Phone in the tray menu, or type 'scan' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: Scan a signed 3-page contract into one PDF to e-mail back.
Keep receipts for your tax return as searchable PDFs instead of paper.
Turn your child's school report into a PDF without a scanner.

do:petal.qr.summary: Makes a QR code for text, a link or a Wi-Fi network, to save as PNG or SVG or copy.
do:petal.qr.details: Create QR Code draws the code as you type. Choose Text or link, or Wi-Fi, where you enter the Network and Password and tick Hidden network if needed; phones that scan it join without typing the password. You can change the two Colours and the Strength (Standard, Strong, Strongest): stronger codes still read when scratched or partly covered, but are denser. Copy Image copies the code, and Save saves it as PNG or SVG, starting in Pictures. Too much text is refused with This is too much text for a QR code.
do:petal.qr.how: It is not on a wheel at first: choose Create QR Code in the tray menu, type 'qr' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K), or copy a link and choose CLIPBOARD on the Quick wheel.
examples: Guests always ask for the Wi-Fi password: print a Wi-Fi QR code and stick it on the fridge.
Put your restaurant's online menu link on table cards.
Add a QR code to a wedding invitation that opens the venue's map link.

do:petal.stats.summary: Shows what DropWheel has done for you: files handled, space saved, petals used and days in a row.
do:petal.stats.details: Your Statistics shows four big numbers: files handled, space saved, petals used and days in a row, with the date counting began and your longest run. Below are a calendar of the last twelve weeks, the petals you used most and your milestones. Everything is counted on this PC only and nothing is sent anywhere. You can untick Keep counting, and Start Over forgets everything after asking.
do:petal.stats.how: It is not on a wheel at first: choose Your Statistics in the tray menu, or type 'statistics' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: See how many gigabytes compressing your phone videos has saved this year.
Find out which petal you use most, to put it first on a wheel.
Check your streak of days in a row using DropWheel.

do:petal.settings.details: DropWheel Settings is DropWheel's main window, and every change is saved at once. It has sections for Keys, Wheels (to change, add or switch off wheels and their petals), Appearance, The Wheel, Screen & Text, Work & Sharing, Actions Wheel, Favourites, Recipes, Automations, Your Petals, Search by Meaning, Results, Quality, Helpers, Statistics, General, Backup and Updates. A new wheel you make starts with this petal on it.
do:petal.settings.how: Choose Settings in the tray menu, choose DROPWHEEL on a wheel where you added it, or type 'settings' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: Change the key that opens the conversion wheel from Shift to another key.
Add the Live Region petal to your Screen wheel under Wheels.
Make a backup of all your wheels and favourites before moving to a new PC.

do:petal.pause.summary: Pauses DropWheel so key taps while dragging no longer open the wheel, until you turn it back on.
do:petal.pause.details: Pause DropWheel makes DropWheel ignore Shift, Ctrl and Alt taps while you drag files, useful in apps where you need those keys mid-drag. A card says DropWheel is paused; choose it again and the card says DropWheel is on again. The petal shows whether DropWheel is paused, and the tray icon's tooltip says so too. The same switch is Pause DropWheel in the tray menu.
do:petal.pause.how: It is not on a wheel at first: right-click the tray icon and choose Pause DropWheel, or type 'pause' in the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K).
examples: Moving layers in Photoshop with Shift held: pause DropWheel so the wheel doesn't appear.
Playing a game that uses Ctrl while dragging: pause DropWheel for the evening.
Copying files in File Explorer with Ctrl held: pause DropWheel for a big tidy-up.

do:text.fixlayout.summary: Puts right text typed with the wrong keyboard language: ؤشف becomes cat, and hgsghl becomes السلام.
do:text.fixlayout.details: Select the garbled text in any app and choose this petal. DropWheel sees which way it went wrong: text that is mostly Arabic letters becomes the English keys under them, and English letters become the Arabic they were meant to be (the US English and Arabic 101 layouts). The fixed text is pasted over the selection, and the keyboard then switches to the language you meant when both layouts are installed, so you can keep typing. DropWheel takes the selection by asking the app through Windows UI Automation, or by copying it with Ctrl+C, and puts your clipboard back as it was afterwards. If the app in front changed meanwhile, the result goes on the clipboard instead ('Copied instead').
do:text.fixlayout.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), press Tab until the Text wheel shows and choose FIX LAYOUT.
examples: You typed a WhatsApp Web message while the keyboard was still on Arabic and got ؤشف: select it and FIX LAYOUT turns it into cat.
A Word line came out as hgsghl ugd;l because English was on: one petal turns it into السلام عليكم.
You typed a Google search with the wrong layout; FIX LAYOUT corrects it and switches the keyboard so the next words come out right.
do:text.fixlayout.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.translate.summary: Translates the selected text on this PC, Arabic and English both ways or into the language DropWheel speaks, to replace or copy.
do:text.translate.details: Select text in any app and choose TRANSLATE: a Translate window opens with the start of the original and the translation in a box you can still edit. Arabic text goes into English and anything else into Arabic; when DropWheel itself is set to Turkish, Persian, Urdu, Indonesian, French or Spanish, text goes into that language instead (or into English when it is already in it). English into Arabic and Arabic into English use the Opus-MT translation models (about 114 MB each) when they are downloaded, a sentence at a time; otherwise, and for the other languages, the AI model Qwen2.5 1.5B (about 1.1 GB) translates; the window offers the download the first time. Replace the Selection pastes the translation over the original text, and Copy puts it on the clipboard. It runs on this PC; the text isn't sent anywhere.
do:text.translate.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel and choose TRANSLATE; then press Replace the Selection or Copy.
examples: An English e-mail from a supplier in Outlook: select it, choose TRANSLATE and read it in Arabic.
You wrote a reply in Arabic in Teams for an English-speaking colleague: TRANSLATE, then Replace the Selection puts the English in its place.
A paragraph on a shopping website is in English: select it in the browser and copy the Arabic translation into your notes.
do:text.translate.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.upper.summary: Turns the selected text into CAPITAL LETTERS, right where it is in any app.
do:text.upper.details: Select text in any app and choose UPPER; every letter becomes a capital and the text is pasted back over the selection. Arabic has no capitals and stays as it is. DropWheel reads the selection through Windows UI Automation, or copies it with Ctrl+C, and puts your clipboard back afterwards. If nothing would change, a card says 'Nothing to change'; if nothing is selected, it says 'No text is selected'.
do:text.upper.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the CASE group and choose UPPER.
examples: A heading in a PowerPoint slide should shout: select 'summer sale' and it becomes 'SUMMER SALE'.
A form asks for your name in capitals: type it normally, select it and choose UPPER.
A product code typed as 'ab-12x' in Excel becomes 'AB-12X' in one step.
do:text.upper.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.lower.summary: Turns the selected text into small letters, right where it is in any app.
do:text.lower.details: Select text in any app and choose LOWER; every capital becomes a small letter and the text is pasted back over the selection. Arabic has no capitals and stays as it is. DropWheel reads the selection through Windows UI Automation, or copies it with Ctrl+C, and puts your clipboard back afterwards. If the text is already all small, a card says 'Nothing to change'.
do:text.lower.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the CASE group and choose LOWER.
examples: You typed a whole paragraph with Caps Lock on in Word: select it and LOWER fixes it.
An e-mail address pasted as 'Sara.Ahmed@Mail.COM' becomes all small letters before you send it.
A shouty line in a chat message, 'PLEASE CALL ME', turns into 'please call me'.
do:text.lower.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.title.summary: Gives every word of the selected text a capital first letter, with the rest small: Title Case.
do:text.title.details: Select text in any app and choose TITLE; each word starts with a capital and the rest of its letters become small, so 'the GREAT gatsby' becomes 'The Great Gatsby'. A new word starts after a space, a hyphen, a bracket, a quote mark or a slash. Because the rest is made small, an abbreviation like NASA becomes Nasa. Arabic has no capitals and stays as it is. The text is pasted back over the selection and your clipboard is put back afterwards.
do:text.title.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the CASE group and choose TITLE.
examples: A book list in Excel typed all in small letters: select the titles and each word gets its capital.
A report heading in Word, 'quarterly sales report', becomes 'Quarterly Sales Report'.
A list of names typed as 'ahmed ali' and 'MONA SAID' becomes 'Ahmed Ali' and 'Mona Said'.
do:text.title.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.sentence.summary: Makes only the first letter of each sentence a capital and the rest small: Sentence case.
do:text.sentence.details: Select text in any app and choose SENTENCE; the first letter after a full stop, ! , ? , the Arabic question mark or a new line becomes a capital, and every other letter becomes small. It is the quickest way to calm text typed in capitals without losing sentence starts. Arabic has no capitals and stays as it is. The text is pasted back over the selection, and DropWheel puts your clipboard back afterwards.
do:text.sentence.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the CASE group and choose SENTENCE.
examples: A customer's message pasted in capitals, 'MY ORDER IS LATE. WHERE IS IT?', becomes 'My order is late. Where is it?'.
Notes typed in small letters in Notepad get a capital at the start of every sentence.
A Title Case paragraph in a Word document reads normally again after one petal.
do:text.sentence.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.diacritics.summary: Removes the harakat (tashkeel), Quranic marks and tatweel from the selected Arabic text.
do:text.diacritics.details: Select Arabic text in any app and choose TASHKEEL; the short-vowel marks (fatha, damma, kasra, sukun, shadda and tanween), the small Quranic marks and the stretching tatweel are taken out, and the letters stay. The cleaned text is pasted back over the selection, and your clipboard is put back as it was. Text without any of these marks gives a 'Nothing to change' card. It is handy before searching, sorting or pasting text into a field that doesn't handle the marks well.
do:text.diacritics.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the TIDY group and choose TASHKEEL.
examples: A fully vowelled poem copied from a website into Word: TASHKEEL leaves plain letters that are easier to edit.
A name written as مُحَمَّد in an Excel sheet doesn't match a search for محمد; remove the marks and it does.
A heading stretched with tatweel like عـــروض becomes عروض again.
do:text.diacritics.worksOn: Arabic text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.digits.summary: Swaps the digits in the selected text: Arabic ١٢٣ become 123, or 123 become ١٢٣.
do:text.digits.details: Select text in any app and choose DIGITS. When the text has any Arabic-Indic (or Persian) digits, they all become 0 to 9, and the Arabic decimal and thousands marks become a full stop and a comma; when it has none, 0 to 9 become ٠ to ٩. The text is pasted back over the selection, and your clipboard is put back afterwards. Other characters are left as they are.
do:text.digits.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the TIDY group and choose DIGITS.
examples: A phone number written as ٠٥٠١٢٣٤٥٦٧ won't go into a website form: DIGITS turns it into 0501234567.
Prices in an Excel column typed with ١٢٫٥ become 12.5 so Excel can add them.
An Arabic letter in Word should show ٢٠٢٦ instead of 2026: select the year and swap it.
do:text.digits.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.tidy.summary: Cleans the selected text: double spaces, spaces at line ends and extra empty lines taken out.
do:text.tidy.details: Select text in any app and choose TIDY. Runs of spaces and tabs become one space, spaces at the start and end of each line go, no more than one empty line is kept in a row, and empty lines at the start and end are removed. Because spaces at line starts go too, indenting is lost. The tidied text is pasted back over the selection, and your clipboard is put back as it was.
do:text.tidy.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel, open the TIDY group and choose TIDY.
examples: Text copied from a PDF into Word comes with double spaces and gaps: TIDY makes it neat in one go.
An e-mail draft in Outlook with five empty lines between paragraphs keeps just one.
A product description pasted into a website form with stray spaces at line ends comes out clean.
do:text.tidy.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.count.summary: Counts the words, characters, lines and sentences in the selected text and shows them on a card.
do:text.count.details: Select text in any app and choose COUNT; a card shows the number of words, then characters, characters without spaces, lines and sentences. Nothing is changed in the text. Arabic and English words are both counted, and emoji count as one character. DropWheel reads the selection through Windows UI Automation or by copying it, and puts your clipboard back afterwards.
do:text.count.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel and choose COUNT.
examples: An essay box allows 500 words: select your draft in the browser and COUNT tells you if it fits.
A tweet or X post must stay under 280 characters: check the character count before posting.
Your Word abstract should have five sentences at most; COUNT shows how many it has.
do:text.count.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.calculate.summary: Works out a selected sum or unit conversion, such as 12% of 340 or 5 km in mi, and copies the answer.
do:text.calculate.details: Select a sum or a conversion in any app and choose CALCULATE; a card shows '= answer' and the answer is copied to the clipboard, while the selected text stays as it is. It reads + - × ÷ ^ and brackets, percentages ('12% of 340', '340 + 12%'), sqrt, sin, cos and tan in degrees, log, ln, abs, round, floor, ceil, pi and e. Conversions cover length, weight, volume, area, speed, data size (KB, MB, GB), time and temperature, written in English or Arabic ('5 km in mi', '٧٠ كغ بالرطل', '98.6 f to c'), and Arabic digits work too.
