Answers keep up to ten significant digits; text it can't read gives 'That isn't a sum'.
do:text.calculate.how: Select the sum, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel and choose CALCULATE; then paste the answer with Ctrl+V.
examples: An invoice in Word says 'VAT 15% of 2,340': select it and the answer 351 is ready to paste.
A recipe asks for 350 f; select '350 f to c' in your notes and get the oven heat in Celsius.
A chat message mentions 1.5 GB in MB; one petal gives 1,500 MB on the clipboard.
do:text.calculate.worksOn: A sum or conversion you select in any app; no files.

do:text.summarize.summary: Writes a short summary of the selected text with the AI model on this PC, to put in place or copy.
do:text.summarize.details: Select text in any app and choose SUMMARY: a Summarize window opens and the AI model Qwen2.5 1.5B writes the summary on this PC. The As switch chooses A few lines (2 or 3 sentences, the default) or Key points (3 to 6 bullet points); changing it writes the summary again. Arabic text is summarized in Arabic and other text in English. The first time, the window offers the model download (about 1.1 GB with its runner). You can edit the result, then Replace the Selection pastes it over the original, or Copy puts it on the clipboard; the text isn't sent anywhere.
do:text.summarize.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel and choose SUMMARY; pick A few lines or Key points, then Replace the Selection or Copy.
examples: A long e-mail thread in Outlook before a meeting: select it and read the key points in a few seconds.
A news article in the browser: SUMMARY gives you two or three sentences to share in a WhatsApp group.
A three-page report in Word: summarize it into bullet points for your manager.
do:text.summarize.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.rewrite.summary: Rewrites the selected text clearer, shorter, more formal, friendlier, or with mistakes fixed, on this PC.
do:text.rewrite.details: Select text in any app and choose REWRITE: a Rewrite window opens and the AI model Qwen2.5 1.5B rewrites it on this PC. The Make it switch offers Clearer (the default), Shorter, Formal, Friendly and Fix mistakes, which corrects spelling, grammar and punctuation and changes nothing else; choosing another one rewrites again. Arabic text is rewritten in Arabic and other text in English. The first time, the window offers the model download (about 1.1 GB with its runner). Edit the result if you like, then Replace the Selection pastes it over the original, or Copy puts it on the clipboard.
do:text.rewrite.how: Select the text, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Text wheel and choose REWRITE; pick a style under Make it, then Replace the Selection.
examples: A message to your landlord in Gmail sounds too blunt: choose Formal and put the polite version in its place.
A cover letter paragraph in Word has typos: Fix mistakes corrects them without changing your words.
A long LinkedIn post: Shorter keeps what matters in half the length.
do:text.rewrite.worksOn: Text you select in any app; no files.

do:text.dictate.summary: Types what you say where the cursor is, in any app, in Arabic, English and many more languages.
do:text.dictate.details: Click where the words should go, then start dictation: a small pill at the bottom of the screen shows a level meter and the time while DropWheel listens. Press the shortcut or DICTATE again, or the tick on the pill, to stop; Esc or the X cancels, and it stops by itself at two minutes. Whisper writes down what you said on this PC and DropWheel types it into the app that was in front; if that app changed, the words go on the clipboard instead. The first time, the Dictation window asks for the speech model: Accuracy Fast (about 60 MB, clear English), Balanced (about 190 MB, the default) or Accurate (about 574 MB, best for Arabic and accents), and Language Detect automatically (the default), العربية, English or many others. It needs a microphone and nothing is sent anywhere.
do:text.dictate.how: Press Ctrl+Win+J in any app, or choose DICTATE on the Text wheel or the Work wheel (Ctrl+Win+Z with no files selected, then Tab); speak, then press it again to type.
examples: Your hands are full: click in a WhatsApp Web chat, press Ctrl+Win+J and say your reply in Arabic.
Write the first draft of a Word report by speaking it in two-minute pieces.
Fill a long comment box on a website by talking instead of typing in English.
do:text.dictate.worksOn: Your voice, typed into any app; no files.

do:window.left.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the left half of its screen.
do:window.left.details: Choose LEFT and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the left half of the screen it is on, above the taskbar. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone; with no app window in front, a card says 'No window to arrange'.
do:window.left.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose LEFT.
examples: Put a Word document on the left and the browser on the right to copy facts across.
Keep a Teams call in the left half while you take notes in OneNote on the right.
Compare two Excel workbooks side by side: LEFT for one, RIGHT for the other.
do:window.left.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.right.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the right half of its screen.
do:window.right.details: Choose RIGHT and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the right half of the screen it is on, above the taskbar. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone; with no app window in front, a card says 'No window to arrange'.
do:window.right.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose RIGHT.
examples: Keep a YouTube tutorial on the right while you follow it in Photoshop on the left.
Put File Explorer on the right to drag files into an e-mail on the left.
Read a PDF on the left and type your answers in Word on the right.
do:window.right.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.top.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the top half of its screen.
do:window.top.details: Choose TOP and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the top half of its screen, across its full width. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. It suits tall or portrait screens. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.top.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose TOP.
examples: On a portrait monitor, keep a chat app in the top half and your code editor below.
Put a wide Excel sheet on top and a Word report underneath to copy numbers down.
Watch a live stream in the top half while reading its chat in the bottom half.
do:window.top.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.bottom.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the bottom half of its screen.
do:window.bottom.details: Choose BOTTOM and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the bottom half of its screen, across its full width and above the taskbar. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.bottom.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose BOTTOM.
examples: Keep a terminal window in the bottom half under your code on a tall screen.
Put WhatsApp Desktop at the bottom while a web page fills the top.
Stack two documents on a portrait monitor: TOP for one, BOTTOM for the other.
do:window.bottom.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.topleft.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the top-left quarter of its screen.
do:window.topleft.details: Choose TOP LEFT and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the top-left quarter of its screen. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With the other quarter petals you can show four windows at once. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.topleft.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose TOP LEFT.
examples: Watch four security camera apps or streams at once, one in each quarter.
Keep Outlook in the top-left corner while three work windows fill the rest.
Put a calculator-sized chat window in the top-left quarter of a big monitor.
do:window.topleft.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.topright.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the top-right quarter of its screen.
do:window.topright.details: Choose TOP RIGHT and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the top-right quarter of its screen. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With the other quarter petals you can show four windows at once. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.topright.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose TOP RIGHT.
examples: Keep Spotify in the top-right corner while you work in the other three quarters.
Put a video call in the top right and shared notes below it.
Arrange four browser windows to compare four hotel prices at once.
do:window.topright.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.bottomleft.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the bottom-left quarter of its screen.
do:window.bottomleft.details: Choose BOTTOM LEFT and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the bottom-left quarter of its screen, above the taskbar. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With the other quarter petals you can show four windows at once. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.bottomleft.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose BOTTOM LEFT.
examples: Keep File Explorer in the bottom-left corner to drag files into the windows above it.
Put a to-do app in the bottom left while e-mail, calendar and chat fill the other quarters.
Show a small timer or music player in a corner during a long work session.
do:window.bottomleft.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.bottomright.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the bottom-right quarter of its screen.
do:window.bottomright.details: Choose BOTTOM RIGHT and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the bottom-right quarter of its screen, above the taskbar. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With the other quarter petals you can show four windows at once. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.bottomright.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose BOTTOM RIGHT.
examples: Keep a Zoom meeting in the bottom-right corner while you share notes in the rest.
Put the Calculator app in the bottom right while you fill an Excel sheet.
Watch a football match in a corner while you keep working on the rest of the screen.
do:window.bottomright.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.leftthird.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the left third of its screen, for wide monitors.
do:window.leftthird.details: Choose LEFT THIRD and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the left third of its screen, full height. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With MIDDLE THIRD and RIGHT THIRD, three windows sit side by side on an ultrawide screen. It isn't on a ready-made wheel: add it from the Arrange windows section in Settings › Wheels, or run Left Third from the command palette.
do:window.leftthird.how: Add LEFT THIRD to a wheel in Settings › Wheels, or press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'Left Third' and press Enter while the app's window is in front.
examples: On an ultrawide monitor, keep Slack in the left third and two work windows beside it.
Put your e-mail on the left third, a document in the middle and the browser on the right.
A narrow chat or music app doesn't need half the screen: a third is enough.
do:window.leftthird.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.middlethird.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the middle third of its screen, for wide monitors.
do:window.middlethird.details: Choose MIDDLE THIRD and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the middle third of its screen, full height. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With LEFT THIRD and RIGHT THIRD, three windows sit side by side on an ultrawide screen. It isn't on a ready-made wheel: add it from the Arrange windows section in Settings › Wheels, or run Middle Third from the command palette.
do:window.middlethird.how: Add MIDDLE THIRD to a wheel in Settings › Wheels, or press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'Middle Third' and press Enter while the app's window is in front.
examples: Keep the document you are writing in the middle of an ultrawide screen, with sources on both sides.
Put a video call in the middle third so you look at the camera, with notes left and right.
Centre your code editor and keep the browser and terminal in the outer thirds.
do:window.middlethird.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.rightthird.summary: Puts the window that was in front into the right third of its screen, for wide monitors.
do:window.rightthird.details: Choose RIGHT THIRD and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills the right third of its screen, full height. A maximised or minimised window is restored first, and its visible frame is fitted exactly. With LEFT THIRD and MIDDLE THIRD, three windows sit side by side on an ultrawide screen. It isn't on a ready-made wheel: add it from the Arrange windows section in Settings › Wheels, or run Right Third from the command palette.
do:window.rightthird.how: Add RIGHT THIRD to a wheel in Settings › Wheels, or press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'Right Third' and press Enter while the app's window is in front.
examples: Keep a to-do list in the right third of an ultrawide monitor all day.
Put the browser with a recipe in the right third while two other windows fill the rest.
Watch a tutorial in the right third while you follow along in the middle.
do:window.rightthird.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.centre.summary: Moves the window that was in front to the middle of its screen, keeping its size.
do:window.centre.details: Choose CENTRE and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel is placed in the middle of its screen at the size it has. A maximised window is restored first. A window bigger than about 92% of the screen shrinks to fit, and a very small one (under 200 by 150 pixels) is made 60% wide and 70% tall. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.centre.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose CENTRE.
examples: A Settings window opened in a corner of a big monitor: CENTRE brings it where you look.
Present a single app in the middle of the screen during a screen share.
An app window partly off the screen after unplugging a monitor comes back to the middle.
do:window.centre.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.maximize.summary: Makes the window that was in front fill its screen, or puts it back to its size.
do:window.maximize.details: Choose MAXIMIZE and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel fills its screen; choose it again and it goes back to its earlier size. The middle of the wheel shows whether that window is maximised now. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone; with no app window in front, a card says 'No window to arrange'.
do:window.maximize.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel and choose MAXIMIZE.
examples: A small Excel window needs the whole screen to see more rows: one petal maximises it.
Make a video player fill the screen without hunting for its button.
Put a maximised browser back to a window so you can see the desktop beside it.
do:window.maximize.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.nextscreen.summary: Moves the window that was in front to the next screen, in the same place and proportions.
do:window.nextscreen.details: Choose NEXT SCREEN and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel moves to the next monitor, counting from left to right and back to the first. It keeps the same position and size relative to the screen, scaled to the other screen's size, and a maximised window stays maximised. It needs two or more screens; with one, the petal says 'Only one screen'.
do:window.nextscreen.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose NEXT SCREEN.
examples: Send a PowerPoint presentation from your laptop screen to the projector.
Move a Zoom call to the second monitor so your main screen stays free for work.
A window opened on the TV connected by HDMI comes back to your laptop in one step.
do:window.nextscreen.worksOn: The app window in front, with two or more screens; no files.

do:window.ontop.summary: Keeps the window that was in front above all other windows, or lets it go back.
do:window.ontop.details: Choose ON TOP and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel stays above every other window, even when you click elsewhere; choose it again and it behaves normally. The middle of the wheel shows whether that window is on top now. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.ontop.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose ON TOP.
examples: Keep a small Calculator window above the Excel sheet you are checking.
Pin a video call over your work so the faces never disappear behind other windows.
Keep a recipe in the browser on top while you write the shopping list in Notepad.
do:window.ontop.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.seethrough.summary: Makes the window that was in front see-through a step at a time, then solid again.
do:window.seethrough.details: Each time you choose SEE THROUGH, the window that was in front when you opened the wheel becomes more see-through: 85% solid, then 70%, then 55%, and then solid again. A card shows the new level, and the middle of the wheel shows how solid the window is now. You can still click and type in it as usual. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone.
do:window.seethrough.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose SEE THROUGH; choose it again for the next step.
examples: Trace a drawing: make a picture window 55% solid over your drawing app.
Keep a chat window half see-through on top of a video so it doesn't hide the picture.
Copy text from a document visible behind a see-through Notepad window.
do:window.seethrough.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:window.minimize.summary: Sends the window that was in front down to the taskbar.
do:window.minimize.details: Choose MINIMIZE and the window that was in front when you opened the wheel goes down to the taskbar, where you can click it to bring it back. The app keeps running while it is down there. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone; with no app window in front, a card says 'No window to arrange'.
do:window.minimize.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose MINIMIZE.
examples: Someone walks up to your desk: minimise the personal chat window in one move.
Clear a big browser window out of the way to reach files on the desktop.
Tuck a music player into the taskbar while it keeps playing.
do:window.minimize.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.
keywords: get window out of the way

do:window.close.summary: Closes the window that was in front, as its own X button would.
do:window.close.details: Choose CLOSE and DropWheel asks the window that was in front when you opened the wheel to close, exactly like clicking its X. The app can still ask you to save your work first, so nothing is lost without asking. DropWheel's own windows, the desktop and the taskbar are left alone; with no app window in front, a card says 'No window to arrange'.
do:window.close.how: Click the app's window, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Arrange wheel, open the MORE group and choose CLOSE.
examples: Close a pop-up window whose X button is off the screen.
Finish with a Word document and close it; Word still asks to save the changes.
Close a stuck-looking settings window without reaching for the mouse corner.
do:window.close.worksOn: The app window in front; no files.

do:clipboard.history.summary: Opens everything you copied lately, to search, pin and paste again into the app you were using.
do:clipboard.history.details: The Clipboard History window lists the last 30 things you copied (text, pictures and files), newest first with pinned clips on top; only the latest 8 pictures are kept. Type in the search box to find a clip, use the pin button to keep one and the bin button (or Delete) to remove one. Double-click a clip, press Enter or choose Paste, and DropWheel puts it on the clipboard and pastes it with Ctrl+V into the app that was in front; Clear All removes everything except pinned clips. Copies that password managers mark as private are never kept. History is kept while DropWheel runs; only pinned clips are remembered after it closes unless you turn that on, in Settings › Screen & Text.
do:clipboard.history.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Clipboard wheel and choose HISTORY; double-click a clip to paste it.
examples: You copied an address an hour ago and then copied other things: find it in History and paste it into the delivery form.
Pin your IBAN or a standard e-mail reply so it is always one click away.
Paste back a screenshot you copied earlier into a Teams chat after copying text since.
do:clipboard.history.worksOn: What you copied: text, pictures and files; no files needed to open it.

do:clipboard.forget.summary: Clears the clipboard history in one step, keeping only the clips you pinned.
do:clipboard.forget.details: Choose FORGET and every clip in DropWheel's clipboard history is deleted, except the ones you pinned; a card says 'Clipboard history cleared' and 'Pinned clips stay'. It works on DropWheel's history, while Empty Clipboard (CLEAR, under MORE on the Quick wheel) forgets only what is on the clipboard right now. It isn't on a ready-made wheel: add it from the Clipboard section in Settings › Wheels, or run Clear Clipboard History from the command palette.
do:clipboard.forget.how: Press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'Clear Clipboard History' and press Enter, or add FORGET to a wheel in Settings › Wheels.
examples: You copied passwords and bank details from a document: clear the history before lending your laptop.
Before sharing your screen in a meeting, forget the private clips so they don't show in the history.
Start a fresh day with an empty history while your pinned e-mail templates stay.

do:notes.new.summary: Puts a new sticky note on the desktop near the pointer, in any language and colour.
do:notes.new.details: Choose NOTE and a sticky note opens near the pointer, ready to type; Arabic runs right to left by itself. Its band has buttons for a New note, Colour (yellow, green, blue, pink, purple, grey), Keep on top and Delete note, and you can drag it by the band and resize it from the corner. Ctrl+N in a note makes another one. Notes are saved by themselves and come back where they were when DropWheel starts; a deleted note with text can be brought back by clicking the card that appears.
do:notes.new.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Work or Clipboard wheel and choose NOTE, then type.
examples: Jot down a phone number during a call without opening any app.
Keep today's three tasks on a yellow note that stays on top of your work.
Write a reminder in Arabic to call the bank, and it is still there after a restart.

do:notes.toggle.summary: Brings every sticky note out, or tucks them all away while they stay saved.
do:notes.toggle.details: Choose NOTES to hide every sticky note at once, and again to show them all where they were. Hidden notes stay saved, and DropWheel remembers the choice: notes tucked away stay hidden the next time DropWheel starts. When you have no notes yet, it makes a new one. It isn't on a ready-made wheel: add it from the Notes section in Settings › Wheels, or run Show or Hide Notes from the command palette.
do:notes.toggle.how: Press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'Show or Hide Notes' and press Enter, or add NOTES to a wheel in Settings › Wheels.
examples: Hide your notes before sharing your screen in a Zoom meeting, then bring them back after.
Clear the desktop to take a clean screenshot, with the notes back in one step.
Bring all your notes out at the start of the day to check your reminders.

do:work.focus.summary: Starts a focus session: distracting apps go down to the taskbar until it ends, and your minutes are counted.
do:work.focus.details: Choosing FOCUS opens the Focus window: pick a Length of 25 min (the default), 50 min, 90 min or Other, tick the apps that should wait, and tick Mute the sound if you like, then choose Start the Session. During the session a small timer sits at the top right of the screen, with + for five more minutes and X to end it; any ticked app that comes to the front is sent down to the taskbar, with a card saying it waits. When the time is up a chime plays and a card shows your minutes today and how many days in a row you have focused. Choosing FOCUS again ends a session early, and the Do Not Disturb… button opens Windows' own notification settings.
do:work.focus.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Work wheel and choose FOCUS; set the length and apps, then Start the Session.
examples: Study for 50 minutes with Instagram and YouTube in the browser kept out of the way.
Write a report for 25 minutes with Discord and WhatsApp sent to the taskbar whenever they pop up.
Keep a daily streak of focus time and see your minutes when each session ends.

do:work.meeting.summary: Records a meeting, then writes the transcript, a summary, the decisions and action items on this PC.
do:work.meeting.details: Choose MEETING and DropWheel records both the PC's sound and your microphone; a pill at the top shows the time, with a tick to stop and write the notes and an X to cancel, and it is kept out of the meeting's own screen shares. When you stop, Whisper writes the transcript with times, and if the AI model (about 1.1 GB) is on the PC it adds Summary, Decisions and Action items sections. The notes (a Markdown file) and the sound (an M4A file) are saved as 'Meeting date time' in the DropWheel Meetings folder in Documents, and the Meeting Notes window opens with Summary and Transcript views, Copy and Open Folder. It needs a speech model from the Dictation window and FFmpeg; without the AI model, a Write a Summary button lets you add the summary later.
do:work.meeting.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Work wheel and choose MEETING; choose it again or press the tick on the pill to stop.
examples: A one-hour Teams call: get the decisions and who does what without taking notes yourself.
A Zoom lecture in Arabic: keep the full transcript and the sound to study later.
A phone call on speaker at your desk: record it and copy the action items into an e-mail.

do:work.captions.summary: Shows live captions for any video, call or lesson, translated into Arabic as they come, on this PC.
do:work.captions.details: Choose CC and a caption bar appears at the bottom of the screen; drag it anywhere. DropWheel listens to the PC's sound (the default) or the microphone, Whisper writes the words down as they are said, within about half a second (the newest look dimmer until they are sure), and the translation model puts each sentence into Arabic as it goes, with no internet needed. If the PC is too slow for the speech model chosen, a quicker one that is downloaded takes over so the captions keep up. Hover over the bar for its buttons: switch between the PC's sound and the microphone, change what is shown (both, Arabic, the original, or English), or turn the captions off. It needs a speech model from the Dictation window, and the Arabic translation model (about 114 MB) is offered the first time; until it is there, the captions show what was said. Choose CC again to stop.
do:work.captions.how: Press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Work wheel and choose CC; choose it again to turn the captions off.
examples: Watch an English YouTube course and read the Arabic captions under it.
Follow a fast Zoom call in English with the words written on the screen as people speak.
Caption a lecture from the microphone for a classmate who is hard of hearing.

do:steps.record.summary: Records a step-by-step guide while you work: each click with a picture and its words, to save as PDF or Word.
do:steps.record.details: Choose STEPS and a bar at the top of the screen counts the steps while you work; every click, double-click, right-click, typing and shortcut in other apps becomes a step with a picture of the window and a ring where you clicked, and words such as 'Click «Save» in Notepad'. Whatever is typed into a password box is never kept; the step just says 'Type the password'. Press the tick to finish (or choose STEPS again), or X to cancel; it stops by itself at 200 steps. The Step-by-Step Guide window then lets you change the title and each step's words, move steps up or down and remove them, and Save Guide as PDF (the default), Word, Web Page or Markdown into the DropWheel Guides folder in Documents. It isn't on a ready-made wheel: add it from the Work section in Settings › Wheels, or run Record Steps from the command palette.
do:steps.record.how: Press Ctrl+Win+K, type 'Record Steps' and press Enter (or add STEPS to a wheel in Settings › Wheels); do the task, then press the tick on the bar.
examples: Show your parents how to join a video call: record the clicks once and send them a PDF guide.
Write how to submit an expense claim in your company's web system as a Word document for new staff.
Report a software problem to IT with every click and screenshot in order.

do:workspace.save.summary: Saves the apps open now and where their windows sit, to open them all together later.
do:workspace.save.details: Choose SAVE LAYOUT and the Save Workspace window lists the app windows open now (minimised ones aren't included), each ticked; give the workspace a Name (it starts as 'Workspace 1', 'Workspace 2' and so on), untick any you don't want, and choose Save. The workspace then appears under WORKSPACES on the Work wheel and in the command palette. Opening it starts the apps that aren't running and puts every window back where it was, maximised ones maximised; a card says if an app couldn't be opened.
do:workspace.save.how: Arrange your windows, press Ctrl+Win+Z (with no files selected), Tab to the Work wheel, open WORKSPACES and choose SAVE LAYOUT, then Save.
examples: Save 'Study' with the browser on the left and OneNote on the right, and open both in place each evening.
Save 'Work' with Outlook, Teams and Excel arranged on two monitors for every morning.
Save 'Editing' with Premiere, File Explorer and Spotify so one petal sets it all up.
do:workspace.save.worksOn: The app windows open now; no files.

do:petal.guide.summary: Opens the Tools Guide: every tool and action explained, with examples, and a box to say what you want to do.
do:petal.guide.details: The guide lists DropWheel's tools, file actions and the actions of the wheels without files by section. Each one opens to what it does, how to use it, three examples and what it works on, with Try It to start it and a box to ask about it. Type what you want to do in your own words at the top and the closest tools appear at once; press Enter and the AI model on this PC answers from the guide and links the tools it names. The model downloads once, the first time you ask; without it the closest tools still appear.
do:petal.guide.how: Open it from the tray menu (Tools Guide…), the Tools Guide button at the top of DropWheel's settings, the command palette (Ctrl+Win+K), or a GUIDE petal you add to a wheel. In a wheel, the mark under a petal's name (or F1) shows that petal's explanation, with a link to the guide.
examples: You need a countdown for a class break: type "countdown" and Timer comes first, with Try It to start it.
You want a PDF small enough for an e-mail: ask "make a PDF smaller" and the guide points to Compress and how to use it.
You aren't sure what Live Region is for: open it under Screen and read the examples, or ask "can it show a video call while I work?".

kind:destination.summary: Copies or moves the files you drop on it straight into a folder you chose, on the actions wheel.
kind:destination.details: A folder petal sits on the actions wheel (Alt while dragging) beside the actions. Dropping files on it copies them into that folder, or moves them, as you set it up; the folder's own name is on the petal. You add, change and remove these folders under Settings › Actions Wheel, where each one says whether it copies or moves. Up to four folders fit on the wheel with the actions.
kind:destination.how: Drag files, tap Alt and drop them on the folder's petal. Add folders in Settings › Actions Wheel.
examples: Invoices that arrive in Downloads: drop each one on an Accounting petal and it is moved there.
Photos to back up: drop them on a petal for your external drive's Photos folder and they are copied.
Finished designs for a client: a Delivered petal moves them out of your work folder in one drop.
kind:destination.worksOn: Any files and folders, one or many.
